findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Key Budgetary Risks, 22/06/2026 Finance Scrutiny Committee, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Business rates reset in 2026/27 will redistribute funding; Watford currently protected
findings.detail: Government has committed to reset business rates and redistribute local authority funding from 2026/27. Watford is currently in a safety net position, protecting it from losses below its pre-determined baseline (first 7.5% is council's responsibility). Likelihood 3, impact 2, score 6.
findings.matters: The imminent 2026/27 business rates reset is a structural funding change. If revised safety net arrangements are less generous, or if Watford's baseline is reset downward, income could fall significantly.
findings.figures: Likelihood 3, Impact 2, Overall Score 6; Council covers first 7.5% loss on baseline
findings.quote: The Council is legally obliged to cover the first 7.5% loss on its pre-determined baseline level. The Council is currently in a safety net position. The Government has committed to a reset of business rates from 2026/27 alongside redistribution of funding for local authorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Key Budgetary Risks, 22/06/2026 Finance Scrutiny Committee, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Government grant funding faces adverse change risk
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy includes prudent forecasts for government grants, but flags central funding reduction as a high-likelihood, high-impact risk (likelihood 4, impact 3, score 12), reflecting ongoing uncertainty in local authority funding from central government.
findings.matters: Central government grant typically funds around half of local authority budgets. Reduction forces immediate service cuts or reserves depletion, both of which constrain council resilience.
findings.figures: Likelihood 4, Impact 3, Overall Score 12
findings.quote: The MTFS includes a prudent forecast for grant funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Key Budgetary Risks, 22/06/2026 Finance Scrutiny Committee, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Commercial property rental income is a major income source under economic pressure
findings.detail: Rental income from the council's property portfolio represents a significant proportion of total council income. Economic downturn is increasing risk; the council notes tenants going into administration. Portfolio is monitored by a Property Investment Board with external advisors (LSH). Rated as high risk: likelihood 4, impact 3, score 12.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is material to the council's revenue base. Loss of multiple tenants through administration would create a direct funding gap that cannot easily be replaced.
findings.figures: Likelihood 4, Impact 3, Overall Score 12
findings.quote: The rental income received from the Councils property portfolio is a significant proportion of the total income the Council receives. The economic climate has increased risk as evidenced by tenants going into administration.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Key Budgetary Risks, 22/06/2026 Finance Scrutiny Committee, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: General fund balance risks falling below risk-assessed level, preventing service delivery
findings.detail: Watford's corporate risk register (item 7) flags that the general fund balance could fall below the council's assessed safe level, preventing delivery of commitments in the Corporate Delivery Plan. Rated as high risk: likelihood 3, impact 4, score 12.
findings.matters: A general fund balance below safe levels indicates the council cannot absorb financial shocks or deliver planned services — a fundamental solvency concern for lenders.
findings.figures: Likelihood 3, Impact 4, Overall Score 12
findings.quote: In that the general fund balance falls below the risk assessed level and the Council is unable to deliver commitments set out in the Corporate Delivery Plan.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring report for Cabinet, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation forcing £0.184m revenue cost that normally would be capital-charged; described as 'ongoing and growing requirement' for 2026/27 onwards.
findings.detail: Project management team costs that would normally be charged to capital projects had to be charged to revenue because of LGR work diversion. The CFO notes this was 'the main driver in the change in financial outturn from P10 to year end' and that 'As part of the 2026/27 budget setting process funding has been set in place for 2026/27 to support this ongoing and growing requirement.' The shift from capital to revenue charging, and the language about 'growing requirement,' suggests this cost will persist and may increase.
findings.matters: Unfunded LGR costs that cannot be capital-charged force councils to absorb them in revenue, consuming resources otherwise available for service delivery or reserve building. A 'growing requirement' signals escalating pressure.
findings.figures: £0.184m revenue overspend in 2025/26 for LGR-related project management; funding for 2026/27 onwards set in place
findings.quote: This team have been diverted to work on the Local government reorganisation (LGR) which has resulted in a revenue overspend of £0.184m as the costs for this work cannot be charged to capital. The main driver in the change in financial outturn from P10 to year end, is related to the resources required to supporting the response to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), both supporting the internal and external programme support. As part of the 2026/27 budget setting process funding has been set in place for 2026/27 to support this ongoing and growing requirement.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring report for Cabinet, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £14.611m in single year; council undertaking financial policy review to 'improve future financial resilience'.
findings.detail: Opening earmarked reserves on 1 April 2025 were £80.398m; approved budgeted allocations of £14.611m were made to support revenue expenditure during 2025/26, reducing closing balance to £65.787m (18% reduction in one year). The paper states closing reserve balance is 'significantly lower' and notes the council is 'currently undertaking a review of capital financing policy...to support reserves overall and improve WBC future financial resilience.' This language signals the council views its reserve position as requiring active management rather than stable.
findings.matters: Persistent use of earmarked reserves to fund revenue spending indicates the operating budget is not self-sustaining. A council drawing reserves at this rate may face structural deficit; the council's own statement that it is seeking to 'improve financial resilience' acknowledges this concern.
findings.figures: £14.611m earmarked reserves allocated to support revenue; Earmarked reserves reduced from £80.398m to £65.787m; General Fund Reserve at risk-assessed level of £3.954m
findings.quote: The closing reserve balance on 31 March 2026 is significantly lower as approved budgeted reserve allocations of £14.611m have been made to support revenue expenditure. The Council is currently undertaking a review of capital financing policy The surplus revenue financing budget generated by this change will be transferred into reserves, to support reserves overall and improve WBC future financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring report for Cabinet, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Watford Business Park lettings shortfall generating £0.764m property overspend; council plans to draw Commercial risk reserve in 2026/27 to manage shortfall.
findings.detail: Property & Asset Management overspent by £0.764m, primarily due to lower than anticipated rental income recovery at Watford Business Park ('the site is not fully let') and £0.482m in costs relating to empty properties. The council acknowledges explicit risk: 'There is a risk that lettings will be slower than projected because of market conditions. As the owner of the site, the Council is liable for service charges and business rates on vacant units.' The 2026/27-2028/29 MTFS assumes the Commercial risk reserve will be utilised to manage this income shortfall.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is discretionary and market-dependent. A development that is not fully let after two years and forces reserve draws to manage the shortfall signals either overoptimistic appraisal assumptions or deteriorating market conditions, both material to lending decisions.
findings.figures: £0.764m Property & Asset Management overspend; £0.482m empty property costs; Commercial risk reserve earmarked for 2026/27 shortfall management
findings.quote: The Property & Asset Management service had an overspend for the year totalling £0.764m, this is largely due to lower than anticipated recovery of rental income for units at Watford Business Park as the site is not fully let and costs relating to empty properties of £0.482m. There is a risk that lettings will be slower than projected because of market conditions. As the owner of the site, the Council is liable for service charges and business rates on vacant units. The 2026/27 to 2028/29 MTFS includes assumptions that the Commercial risk reserve will be utilised to manage the short-term shortfall in income in 2026/27 whilst vacant units are let.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring report for Cabinet, 01/07/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand overspend of £0.464m expected to persist; council signals need for 'careful management and monitoring' into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Housing service overspent by £0.464m in temporary accommodation due to rising demand driven by private landlord exits, no-fault evictions, and shortage of affordable housing supply. External agencies have caused unknown delays to affordable housing delivery at four sites (Sydney Road, Northcott's, Cygnet, Plover). The council explicitly acknowledges this is 'an ongoing challenge for local authorities' requiring ongoing management, and recognises a net pressure of £0.703m in the 2025/26 to 2027/28 Medium Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory duty with demand uncontrollable by the council. Persistent overspends driven by external factors (housing market, evictions) signal a structural mismatch between duty and affordability that may require ongoing reserve draws or service cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: £0.464m temporary accommodation overspend; £0.703m net pressure recognised in 2025/26 to 2027/28 MTFS
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation is an ongoing challenge for local authorities and managing demand and ensuring supply is a national concern that will require very careful management and monitoring in 26/27 and beyond. Unknown delays to affordable housing provision provided by external agencies expected in year at Sydney Road, Northcott's, Cygnet and Plover are the significant contributor to the overspend over planned budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Spend on temporary accommodation remains high and continues to be managed via ongoing arrangements
findings.detail: The council identifies high temporary accommodation spend as an ongoing issue, noting it is nationally the case, and states it is being addressed through service transformation and improvement with weekly management information and training plans.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory pressure on many councils. Watford identifies it as continuing high spend, suggesting it remains a material operational cost pressure and area of focus for management.
findings.figures: Ongoing; weekly management information being tracked
findings.quote: Spend on temporary accommodation continues to be high, as is nationally the case. The ongoing transformation and improvement of the housing service seeks to continue to improve management and performance in this area of work.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer role moved to shared service arrangement with Dacorum BC, effective February 2026
findings.detail: In January 2026, the council approved appointment of Dacorum's existing Section 151 Officer to serve Watford under a Section 113 shared service agreement, commencing 1 February 2026. This represents a recent change to a key finance leadership position that came after audits were already disclaimed.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer is the statutory finance lead responsible for financial administration and reporting. A shared arrangement started during an audit recovery period is a material governance change a lender would need to understand.
findings.figures: Arrangement commenced 1 February 2026; approved 27 January 2026
findings.quote: In January 2026, Council approved the appointment of the existing Section 151 Officer at Dacorum Borough Council as the shared Section 151 for Watford and the arrangement formally commenced on 1 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Four consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions mean accounts remain unverified by external audit
findings.detail: The accounts for 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25 have all received disclaimed audit opinions due to audit delays and backstop dates. The council says it will work with external audit to rebuild assurance from 2025/26 onwards, but this means a lender cannot currently verify the council's financial position from independently audited accounts.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess the council's true financial position or asset values when external audit has disclaimed their opinions on four consecutive years of accounts.
findings.figures: Four years of accounts (2021/22 through 2024/25)
findings.quote: The delay to the audit of the 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 accounts has impacted on the timeliness of financial reporting. The implementation of the backstop dates resulted in a disclaimed audit opinion for 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24. Due to a build back of the accounts being required by audit a disclaimed opinion was given for 2024/25. Officers will work with external audit to rebuild assurance through the 2025/26 audit onwards.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - External Audit Plan - 2025.26
findings.headline: Council assessed at 'higher end of risk spectrum' for building back assurance; requires full substantive testing of income and expenditure
findings.detail: The statutory risk assessment (LARRIG 06) concludes the Council is at 'the higher end of the risk spectrum for building back assurance' following four years of disclaimed opinions. This triggers 'full procedures over the Council's income and expenditure transactions...over the disclaimed period.' This indicates the control environment was sufficiently weak that sample-based testing is insufficient; 100% substantive verification is required.
findings.matters: A high-risk rebuild classification signals control deficiencies extend across core income and expenditure processes, not isolated to complex estimates. Recovery to a clean opinion is multi-year and not assured.
findings.figures: Build-back period: 2021/22 through 2024/25 (four years)
findings.quote: Our initial indications from this work are that the Council is at the higher end of the risk spectrum for building back assurance. This means full procedures over the Council's income and expenditure transactions will be required over the disclaimed period.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - External Audit Plan - 2025.26
findings.headline: Council recently reduced Minimum Revenue Provision charge through methodology change; auditors flagging prudence concerns
findings.detail: The audit plan identifies as a 'High' inherent risk that 'The Council recently changed its approach to the calculation of MRP which resulted in a significant reduction in the annual charge.' Auditors will specifically evaluate 'whether the Council may not have been appropriately prudent in its calculation of MRP and/or not followed the relevant statutory guidance.' This suggests the council tightened MRP policy to ease budget pressure rather than for justified accounting reasons.
findings.matters: MRP is a mandatory statutory charge that funds future repayment of borrowing. Reducing it without proper justification is aggressive accounting that understates the council's true future liabilities and could mask unsustainable borrowing levels.
findings.figures: Reduction amount not disclosed; described as 'significant'
findings.quote: The Council recently changed its approach to the calculation of MRP which resulted in a significant reduction in the annual charge. There is a risk that the Council may not have been appropriately prudent in its calculation of MRP and/or not followed the relevant statutory guidance.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - External Audit Plan - 2025.26
findings.headline: Croxley Park income strip has significantly underperformed against business plan and threatens going concern
findings.detail: The Council entered a 'complex and financially significant' income strip scheme that is 'significantly underperforming compared to the business plan and initial income projections.' If losses continue and the scheme fails to generate sufficient income to cover lease payments, 'this could create a mismatch between the Council's liabilities and its income from the asset' and 'could in turn negatively impact the Council's overall financial position.' Going concern is explicitly flagged as a risk.
findings.matters: A material income stream underpinning the council's financial plan is failing to deliver. This directly threatens the council's ability to service its liabilities and signals potential need for reserve drawdown or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Underperformance described as 'significant' but quantum not disclosed in audit plan
findings.quote: The income strip has significantly underperformed compared to the business plan and initial income projections. If the income strip continues to make losses and is not generating sufficient income in the medium to longer term to cover the lease payments to the Council, this could create a mismatch between the Council's liabilities and its income from the asset.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - External Audit Plan - 2025.26
findings.headline: Four consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions on the Council's financial statements
findings.detail: Watford has received disclaimed opinions for 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. This means there is 'limited assurance available over the Council's opening balances' and 'Significant transactions, accounting treatment and management judgements may not have been subject to audits for one or more years – or at all.' The auditors describe this as creating a 'Very High' inherent risk of material misstatement at financial statement level.
findings.matters: Four consecutive years of audit failure means the Council's financial position and sustainability cannot be reliably verified. This is a critical risk signal for any lender evaluating credit quality.
findings.figures: Four years of disclaimers: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: Disclaimed audit opinions have also been provided on the Council's accounts for the 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 financial years. As a result of the backstop implemented on 27 February 2026, a disclaimer audit opinion was provided on the Council and Group's 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Mid-Year Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council has £13.7m committed to Hart Homes Watford Ltd, representing 61% of £22.5m non-treasury investment portfolio
findings.detail: The council holds £2.400m in equity and £11.301m in loans to Hart Homes Watford Ltd, alongside additional service/commercial investments including £2.000m to West Herts Hospital Trust (Infrastructure) and £6.352m in Watford Health Campus Partnership Loan Notes. These non-treasury investments represent significant capital commitments concentrated in a small number of council-controlled or council-backed entities.
findings.matters: These investments tie up material council capital and create concentration risk. Performance of Hart Homes directly affects £13.7m of council assets. This capital commitment competes for resources with other priorities as the council transitions to external borrowing.
findings.figures: Total non-treasury investments £22.461m: Hart Homes Watford Ltd equity £2.400m + loans £11.301m (£13.701m = 61% of total), West Herts Hospital Trust £2.000m, Watford Health Campus £6.352m, other £0.408m.
findings.quote: The Council also held £22.461m of such investments in Equity in Hart Homes Watford Ltd - £2.400m Loans to Hart Homes Watford Ltd - £11.301m Loan to West Herts Hospital Trust (Infrastructure) - £2.000m Watford Health Campus Partnership Loan Notes - £6.352m

findings.paper_title: Mid-Year Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Watford to raise £20m of external borrowing before end of 2025-26
findings.detail: The council has maintained a strategy of internal borrowing and deferred external debt while managing day-to-day liquidity, but now anticipates requiring £20m of new external borrowing before the end of the financial year. This represents a shift from internal to external financing. The cost of the borrowing is expected to fall within existing budgets.
findings.matters: Lenders track when councils access capital markets; this signals Watford's move from internal reserves to external debt and its implications for debt profile and servicing capacity.
findings.quote: There was no new borrowing during the period, but new borrowing of £20m is anticipated to be required before the end of the 2025-26 financial year. The cost of new borrowing will fall within existing budgets.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Staff turnover and capacity issues in key finance functions causing audit delays
findings.detail: Delays arose in receiving responses from Revenue & Benefits and Property teams due to unplaced staff turnover and periods of leave. This reduced the time available for resolving follow-up queries and progressing other areas of the audit.
findings.matters: Staff turnover in core finance functions directly impacts the council's ability to prepare reliable accounts and respond to audit queries. Capacity issues suggest the finance team may be understaffed for the complexity of the council's accounts.
findings.figures: Delays from unplanned staff turnover; Finance team delays from 'time required to work through queries'
findings.quote: We also encountered delays in receiving responses from the Revenue & Benefits and the Property team, these were primarily caused by limited capacity resulting from unplanned staff turnover and periods of leave.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Property revaluation omission: land and building assets revaluation posting was not captured in financial statements; variances between fixed asset register and valuer's report
findings.detail: During audit of property valuations, auditors found that the revaluation posting relating to land and building assets revalued by Sanderson Weatherall was omitted and therefore not captured in the financial statements. Additionally, there are variances between the fixed asset register and valuer's report that remain unresolved, with delays from the valuer exceeding one month.
findings.matters: Omitted revaluations directly affect the balance sheet accuracy. Unresolved variances between asset register and valuations indicate control failures in fixed asset management, a material area of the balance sheet.
findings.figures: One revaluation posting omitted from financial statements; variances between fixed asset register and valuer's report unresolved
findings.quote: we have reported a finding, as the revaluation posting relating to land and building assets revalued by Sanderson Weatherall was omitted and therefore not captured in the financial statements

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Croxley Business Park Income Strip (complex finance lease arrangement) remains incomplete and unaudited; auditors unable to conclude on valuation or discount rate
findings.detail: The council entered a complex income strip scheme. Auditors have not received the valuation report for the asset at lease inception, which is needed to determine the discount rate used in calculating the lease liability. Work on this arrangement remains ongoing at year-end and will be concluded in 2025/26. This is a significant balance affecting multiple areas of the accounts.
findings.matters: This is a materially significant, complex transaction with management estimates that auditors cannot verify. Unaudited complex arrangements are a red flag for potential misstatement affecting the balance sheet and reserves.
findings.figures: Inherent risk of material misstatement: Very High
findings.quote: We are currently confirming with management whether the asset has been valued at lease inception or not. From understanding of the workings provided, the lease liability has been calculated by discounting the minimum lease payments using a "deemed" incremental borrowing rate instead of using the interest rate implicit in the lease. We are unable to conclude on this until we have received further evidence and confirmation from management. As our procedures are ongoing at the time of writing we are not yet able to conclude over the accuracy and reasonableness of the accounting estimate in the initial valuation and the expected interest rate used.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: £6.5m of material adjustments required to financial statements identified during audit; draft accounts contained high number of errors including material errors
findings.detail: The auditors identified 4 adjustments resulting in a £6.5m improvement to reported outturn. The draft accounts issued 30 June 2025 were substantially amended and re-issued 29 September 2025 with multiple material errors, formula errors and inconsistencies in notes and supporting workings, indicating weaknesses in the council's quality assurance processes.
findings.matters: Material errors requiring adjustment suggest control weaknesses in financial reporting. The extent of errors and need for substantial re-issue indicates the council's accounts preparation process is unreliable.
findings.figures: 4 adjustments = £6.5m improvement; re-issue date 29 September 2025 (3 months after initial draft); high number of errors identified including material errors, formula errors, and inconsistencies
findings.quote: From the work we have completed, we have identified 4 adjustments to the financial statements that have resulted in a £6.5m improvement to your reported financial outturn... we identified a high number of errors, which includes material errors, formula errors, and inconsistencies within the notes and supporting workings. This level of error indicates weaknesses in the Council's quality assurance processes over the preparation of the draft accounts.

findings.paper_title: Watford Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Auditors intend to disclaim opinion on 2024/25 financial statements; no assurance can be given on the accounts
findings.detail: The auditors have concluded they cannot issue an unmodified audit opinion due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026 preventing completion of all necessary procedures. Combined with prior years' disclaimed opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24), there is no assured opening balance position and insufficient assurance over material balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the financial statements provide no audited assurance to lenders or the council's finance director—they cannot rely on the numbers to make lending or financial decisions.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026. Three prior years disclaimed. £6.5m in adjustments identified.
findings.quote: it is not possible for us to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026. Undertaking work on balances that have not been subject to audit for several years necessarily means the audit on the current year balances takes longer than would ordinarily be the case. The limitations imposed from this lack of assurance on opening balances and closing balances in key areas means we are unable to form an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. We therefore intend to disclaim our opinion.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 2. Capital Strategy - 2026-27 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Croxley Park finance lease (£270m liability) remeasured upward £11.222m under IFRS 16 in 2024-25; council has made £1.249m voluntary overpayments to manage accounting volatility
findings.detail: The council's largest single liability, a £270.068m finance lease for Croxley Business Park acquired in July 2019, underwent an £11.222m upward remeasurement in 2024-25 due to IFRS 16 lease accounting. The council has accumulated £1.249m in voluntary revenue provision specifically to mitigate accounting risks and volatility around this lease, indicating recognition of material balance sheet exposure.
findings.matters: Lease accounting changes create balance sheet volatility and unpredictable budget impacts; further remeasurements could require additional revenue provisions, and the £275m liability constrains the council's debt capacity
findings.figures: Lease liability £270.068m; 2024-25 remeasurement £11.222m; cumulative voluntary overpayments to date £1.249m
findings.quote: In July 2019, the Council acquired Croxley Park (a local business park) through a finance lease. Under proper accounting practice for finance lease arrangements, both the asset and lease liability are recognised on the Council's balance sheet. The finance lease is a debt instrument.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 2. Capital Strategy - 2026-27 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Earmarked revenue reserves available for capital drop from £10.257m to zero within two years, eliminating financial flexibility
findings.detail: Capital funding from reserves falls from £10.257m (2025-26) to £0.179m (2026-27) to zero from 2027-28 onwards. Once depleted, capital expenditure becomes entirely dependent on borrowing or external grants, removing the council's ability to manage underfunded emergencies or tactical deployment of cash.
findings.matters: Loss of reserves removes the council's financial cushion; from 2027-28 onwards, all capital funding must come from borrowing, restricting strategic flexibility and increasing vulnerability to external shocks
findings.quote: Revenue balances from the General Fund may be used to directly fund capital expenditure. This also includes contributions from revenue Earmarked Reserves.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 2. Capital Strategy - 2026-27 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Annual financing costs forecast to reach £1.436m in 2026-27 (7.56% of net revenue), nearly tripling from 2025-26 and consuming increasing revenue capacity
findings.detail: The cost of capital jumps from £0.515m (2.96% of revenue) in 2025-26 to £1.436m (7.56% of revenue) in 2026-27 as the council shifts from using reserves to external borrowing to fund capital expenditure. This is the highest ratio in the forecast period. The sharp increase reflects growing external debt service obligations as internal resources deplete.
findings.matters: At 7.56% of net revenue, financing costs constrain borrowing capacity; further deterioration or interest rate rises would severely limit the council's ability to fund capital investment or service emergencies
findings.quote: Where the Council decides to borrow to fund capital expenditure the annual cost of borrowing is included within the revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 2. Capital Strategy - 2026-27 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Commercial property and investment income represents 60.95% of net revenue in 2026-27, creating exceptional concentration risk
findings.detail: The council's £18.998m net revenue stream in 2026-27 includes £11.580m from commercial investments. This ratio has fallen from 65.68% in 2024-25 but remains exceptionally high compared to typical councils. Revenue sustainability now depends critically on property valuations, rental income, and tenant covenant strength rather than on service delivery or statutory funding.
findings.matters: A property market downturn, rental arrears, or tenant defaults would directly force service reductions or emergency borrowing, making the council's financial position unusually vulnerable to commercial real estate cycles
findings.figures: £11.580m from £18.998m net revenue = 60.95%
findings.quote: Net income from commercial investments comprises net income from financial investments (other than treasury management investments), together with net income from other assets held primarily for financial return, such as commercial property.

findings.paper_title: Appointment of Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Local Government Reform severely constrains ability to recruit quality senior finance officers
findings.detail: Market testing over 12 months with leading recruitment agencies revealed that attracting quality candidates to councils undergoing local government reform is extremely difficult regardless of salary. Senior officer fees have increased significantly and quality candidates remain scarce, explaining why Watford resorted to a shared arrangement with another council rather than recruiting a dedicated CFO.
findings.matters: This context explains the structural choice to share a CFO rather than recruit independently, signaling broader resource constraints and governance instability in the sector that could affect financial oversight capacity.
findings.figures: 12 months of market testing conducted
findings.quote: Attracting quality candidates to a council like Watford, which is undergoing local government reform, would be incredibly challenging, regardless of salary. Additionally, the fees attracted by senior officers have increased significantly, and quality candidates are also scarce.

findings.paper_title: Appointment of Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer has resigned; replacement to be appointed from Dacorum as shared arrangement from 1 February 2026
findings.detail: Watford's existing Section 151 Officer resigned, and the council proposes appointing Nigel Howcutt, currently S151 Officer at Dacorum Borough Council, to the role effective 1 February 2026. Howcutt will work part-time and be supported by Watford's shared Head of Finance and finance team, while remaining employed by Dacorum under section 113 of the Local Government Act 1972.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer holds statutory responsibility for proper administration of the council's financial affairs, including audit relationships and government returns. A change in this role and structure affects governance stability and continuity.
findings.figures: Effective from 1 February 2026
findings.quote: Following discussions with Dacorum Borough Council, it is proposed that Nigel Howcutt, the existing Section 151 Officer at Dacorum, is appointed as the Section 151 Officer and CFO to Watford Borough Council, effective from 1 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council Tax frozen while inflation runs at 3.8%, limiting revenue growth
findings.detail: The Band D charge for 2026/27 is frozen at £308.51 (no increase), despite RPI inflation of 3.8% in November 2025. The council has the flexibility to raise council tax by up to 3% or £5 (whichever is greater), but has chosen not to use it. This forgoes approximately £0.936m in potential revenue (0.11% of net expenditure × £308.51 × tax base). Future years forecast 1.99% increases, also below inflation.
findings.matters: Freezing council tax while costs rise by 3.8% is a deliberate choice to absorb real-terms spending cuts or rely on reserves and savings. It limits the council's ability to raise revenue and signals either political constraints on tax rises or concern about taxpayer affordability (a sign of a weaker economic area).
findings.figures: Band D charge £308.51 (frozen); RPI inflation 3.8%; planned increase 2027/28 and 2028/29 at 1.99% (below forecast inflation)
findings.quote: The average Band D Council Tax charge for 2026/27 is proposed to be £308.51, frozen at 2025/26 levels. This compares to a rate of inflation of 3.8% in November 2025 as measured by the Retail Price Index (RPI).

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation (LGR) will occur during the MTFS period, creating planning uncertainty
findings.detail: LGR is expected during the current parliamentary term. The council has made contingency provision for LGR costs but flags material risk. The CFO identifies risks including duplication of costs during transition, delays in service redesign, uncertainty in resource allocation, and impact on staff retention and service delivery. The timing and scope are not yet settled.
findings.matters: Structural change to local government during a three-year budget period is a major source of execution risk. It undermines the reliability of both savings assumptions and cost forecasts. Staff uncertainty during a restructure typically worsens service performance and increases costs.
findings.figures: LGR expected during current parliamentary term (2024–2029); contingency provision made but amount not separately itemised
findings.quote: The timing and scope of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) present risks to financial stability and planning assumptions. While LGR offers opportunities for improved funding and strategic investment, the transition period may lead to duplication of costs, delays in service redesign and uncertainty in resource allocation.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Budget depends on draw-down from Collection Fund Reserve to balance in all three years
findings.detail: The MTFS includes planned release of accumulated retained business rates income from the Collection Fund Reserve in 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29 to bring the budget into balance. A forecast balance of £0.969m will remain on the reserve by March 2029. The CFO notes that 'ongoing savings in the region of £1.000m will be required to remove this reliance on reserve funding.' This is a structural deficit problem hidden by reserve use.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns to balance a budget signal the council cannot fund recurring expenditure from recurring income. This erodes financial resilience and limits the council's ability to manage future shocks. A £1m annual savings gap will need to be closed eventually.
findings.figures: Reserve draw-down across three years; £0.969m forecast balance remaining at March 2029; £1.000m ongoing savings needed to eliminate reserve reliance
findings.quote: The proposed MTFS includes the release of accumulated retained business rates income from the Collection Fund Reserve in 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29. These drawdowns bring the budget into balance in these years.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Material MTFS savings remain unidentified into the budget year
findings.detail: The council relies on delivering savings across the MTFS, but some savings are 'yet to be identified.' The 2026/27 saving target is 'held centrally and will be allocated to services as savings are identified.' The council explicitly flags a risk that 'savings will not be achieved, particularly in the context of LGR.' This is not a speculative forecast but a recognised gap.
findings.matters: A lender would see unidentified savings as a red flag. It indicates the council cannot yet explain how the budget balances. LGR adds execution risk to savings delivery by creating organisational uncertainty during a critical period.
findings.figures: 2026/27 saving held centrally and unallocated to services
findings.quote: The 2026/27 saving is held centrally and will be allocated to services as savings are identified. However, there is a risk that savings will not be achieved, particularly in the context of LGR.

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio under pressure from tenant failures and slower lettings
findings.detail: The council's Core Investment Portfolio (including Watford Business Park/Aspire) is delivering less income than forecast. Lettings are slower than anticipated and new lettings require short-term incentives. In late 2024, a company operating units at Coleshill Industrial Estate went into liquidation, leaving hazardous materials on site. Full remediation is needed before re-letting, which will involve further short-term incentives and budget pressure.
findings.matters: Commercial income is a material revenue source (11.56% of expenditure according to financial resilience metrics). Tenant insolvency and operational slippage signal weaker market conditions and execution risk. The hazardous materials liability is an unbudgeted tail risk.
findings.figures: Coleshill Industrial Estate tenant liquidation; lettings at Aspire slower than anticipated; new lettings subject to 'short term incentives'
findings.quote: one of the companies occupying a number of units at the Coleshill Industrial Estate went into liquidation. As a result of the hazardous materials used as part of production, a full clean-up of the site is required prior to re-letting

findings.paper_title: Attachment 1. Budget report 2026-29 - Cabinet Final, 19/01/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend driven by prevention service failure and scheme delays
findings.detail: Housing is forecasting a net pressure due to overspend on bed & breakfast and nightly let costs. Prevention outcomes collapsed from 28 per month in Q1 2025/26 to 20 per month in Q2, driving approximately 24 additional households into temporary accommodation. The Northcotts scheme is delayed because the main contractor entered administration. The council has built in budget pressure to be prudent, but demand prevention remains 'very challenging.'
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends are hard to control and threaten financial stability. A faltering prevention service and contractor failure are service delivery risks that a lender would see as indicators of weaker operational control.
findings.figures: 28 per month (Q1 prevention) to 20 per month (Q2); 24 additional households into temporary accommodation; Northcotts scheme delayed from Q2 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: successful prevention outcomes fell from 28 per month in Q1 2025/26 to 20 per month in Q2 which led to approximately 24 additional households entering temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Draft Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Statutory override on pooled fund investment losses expired 31 March 2025; losses now hit the general fund
findings.detail: Section 5.6 discloses that the previous accounting protection for movements in fair value of pooled investments ended on 1 April 2025. The council currently holds no pooled funds but reserves the option. Should they invest in future, market downturns could directly impact the budget. The document acknowledges this creates a constraint on investment strategy.
findings.matters: This regulatory change narrows the council's investment options and creates a new budget risk if they choose to use pooled funds. It is a material constraint on the treasury strategy.
findings.figures: Maximum pooled fund investment limit of £5m is set in the strategy, but not currently used
findings.quote: From 1 April 2025, gains and losses will need to be recognised in the general fund. Although in the long term funds are expected to grow in value, the volatile nature of the bond and equity markets mean that there can be significant movements in value from year to year.

findings.paper_title: Draft Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: External borrowing is expected to increase as the council draws down reserves over the MTFS period
findings.detail: Section 4.4 states that Watford's external debt will rise as it refinances internal borrowing with external loans to fund reserve drawdown. The council is using up revenue and capital reserves for unspecified purposes. This signals a shift in the council's financing model from self-funding to external borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why a council's reserves are being depleted and whether current operations are self-sustaining. Rising external debt coupled with falling reserves is a key indicator of financial stress.
findings.figures: No specific borrowing amounts given; maximum borrowing limits are referenced elsewhere but the expected increase is not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The Council's level of external borrowing is expected to increase over the period of the MTFS as it will be necessary to refinance internal borrowing with external debt as the Council utilises its revenue and capital earmarked reserves for their intended purposes.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators draft for full council
findings.headline: Additional revenue provision is being made for Croxley Business Park lease accounting adjustments.
findings.detail: The revised MRP policy includes Voluntary Revenue Provision to mitigate identified risk arising from lease accounting adjustments related to Croxley Business Park, indicating complexity or risk in this capital asset that requires ongoing financial safeguards.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand capital assets with complex lease arrangements and any identified financial risks the council has flagged.
findings.figures: Not specified in the paper.
findings.quote: disclosure of "Voluntary Revenue Provision" which is an additional provision that will mitigate some risk around MRP that results from lease accounting adjustments required for Croxley Business Park.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators draft for full council
findings.headline: External MRP review results in £1.875m reversal of prior-year overpayments and lower future charges.
findings.detail: MUFG reviewed the council's MRP policy and Capital Financing Requirement. The review prompted policy changes being implemented, with an accounting reversal of £1.875m in prior-year overpayments and reduced MRP charges going forward.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand changes to how the council calculates debt repayment charges, why prior payments were excessive, and the resulting improvement to cash position.
findings.figures: £1.875m reversal of historic MRP overpayments; reduced MRP Charges in the short term
findings.quote: The impact of the changes are a reversal of historic MRP overpayments of £1.875m, and reduced MRP Charges in the short term.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators draft for full council
findings.headline: One Prudential Indicator for Finance Lease debt was set incorrectly and is now being corrected.
findings.detail: The operational boundary for Finance Lease debt was set too low and did not reflect the council's total external debt including other long-term liabilities. This was identified as an error and is being corrected in the revised Capital Strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand control weaknesses in the council's financial monitoring systems, how they were identified, and how they are being addressed.
findings.figures: Not specified in the paper.
findings.quote: There is a breach of one of the indicators reported in 2025/26 – this relates to the operational boundary for Finance Lease debt, which appears to have been set at a level which does not reflect the total external debt including other long-term liabilities in the Capital Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL (002)
findings.headline: Operational boundary error in 2025/26 Capital Strategy on finance lease debt
findings.detail: The operational boundary for finance lease debt was incorrectly set at £100m in the 2025/26 Capital Strategy, a reduction from £275m in 2024/25, despite no planned change in lease debt levels. The council has now corrected it. The actual finance lease debt is £256m, making the £100m boundary unworkable as a management control.
findings.matters: Control failures in financial planning processes raise questions about the reliability of forecasts and the quality of finance function management
findings.figures: Finance lease operational boundary incorrectly set at £100m in 2025/26 (should have been c.£275m); actual lease debt £256m
findings.quote: It appears that an error was made in the preparation of the Capital Strategy for 2025/26; the operational boundary for finance lease debt was changed from £275m in 2024/25 to £100m in 2025/26. As there was no intention to reduce or increase lease debt in the financial plans for 2025/26, this indicator should have been set at a level that allowed for the existing finance lease debt and has therefore been updated as above.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL (002)
findings.headline: Total debt planned to increase from £278.5m to £320m over three years
findings.detail: Debt including PFI and leases is £278.5m at 30 June 2025 and forecast to grow to £290m (March 2026), £305m (March 2027), and £320m (March 2028). This represents 15% growth in total debt over the three-year forecast period.
findings.matters: Significant debt growth requires strong revenue backing and clear capital investment justification; lenders track debt trajectory relative to income

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL (002)
findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 18.1% of net revenue stream by 2026/27
findings.detail: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue increases from 15.58% in 2024/25 to 18.10% in 2026/27, with absolute annual costs rising from £2.41m to £3.13m. This 2.5 percentage point increase within two years indicates growing debt servicing pressure relative to available revenue.
findings.matters: High financing cost ratios squeeze financial flexibility; 18% is approaching levels that concern lenders and restricts capacity for service investment or response to shocks
findings.quote: Financing costs (£m) 2.410 2.709 3.133 3.188; Proportion of net revenue stream 15.58% 15.90% 18.10% 17.93%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL (002)
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to spike to £37.1m in 2025/26 then fall sharply
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure is forecast to jump from £21.6m in 2024/25 to £37.1m in 2025/26, then drop to £19.5m in 2026/27 and £7.9m in 2027/28. The spike is driven by investment in Riverwell and Colosseum refurbishment. This concentrated spending pattern has implications for debt financing and revenue consequences.
findings.matters: Lenders track capital programme stability; large temporary spikes create financing challenges and suggest possible project risk if plans change
findings.quote: The main General Fund capital projects to date have included investment in Riverwell and the refurbishment of the Colosseum.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management End of Year Report 2024/25, 01/10/2025 Audit Committee
findings.headline: IFRS16 accounting treatment added £33m to lease liabilities, exceeding the Authorised Limit approved for the year
findings.detail: Finance Lease debt stood at £256.1m at year-end, exceeding the Authorised Limit of £223.0m by £33.1m due to annual remeasurement requirements under IFRS16. Council describes this as technical but indicates forecasting process underestimated the impact of new accounting standards on balance sheet obligations.
findings.matters: Council's financial planning was inadequate to anticipate the scale of IFRS16's impact on reported liabilities, indicating potential weakness in understanding of balance sheet obligations.
findings.figures: Finance Lease debt £256.1m; Authorised Limit £223.0m; variance £33.1m
findings.quote: The indicator for Finance Lease debt was exceeded during 2024/25 due to technical accounting adjustments required under IFRS16. It is important to note that this remeasured liability is a technical adjustment only, and does not change the amount of cash to be repaid.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management End of Year Report 2024/25, 01/10/2025 Audit Committee
findings.headline: Multiple breaches of treasury management counterparty credit limits during 2024/25
findings.detail: Council held £10.178m with Lloyds Bank against a £10.000m limit overnight in January 2025 due to administrative oversight. Two additional breaches occurred from unexpected in-day cash receipts. Year-end position shows £10.561m in unsecured bank investments against a £10.000m limit, confirming structural non-compliance.
findings.matters: Multiple failures to maintain treasury management controls indicate weakened oversight of counterparty concentration risk, particularly with the council's main banking relationship.
findings.figures: January breach £0.178m; year-end £10.561m against £10.000m limit; three separate breaches during the year
findings.quote: In January 2025, and administrative oversight resulted in a breach of the counterparty limit with the Council's Bank, Lloyds. As a consequence the Council held a total balance of £10.178m with the bank for one night, against a limit of £10.000m.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators FINAL PUBLISHED
findings.headline: Croxley Business Park lease accounting requires additional voluntary revenue provision to mitigate MRP risk.
findings.detail: The MRP policy changes include a disclosure of Voluntary Revenue Provision to address risks arising from IFRS 16 lease accounting adjustments for Croxley Business Park. This suggests the asset has complex lease structures requiring financial provisions beyond standard accounting treatment.
findings.matters: Complex lease arrangements can mask underlying liabilities and cash flow requirements. The need for additional provisions suggests the asset carries risks that warrant closer scrutiny from lenders.
findings.figures: Voluntary Revenue Provision required; no amount disclosed
findings.quote: disclosure of "Voluntary Revenue Provision" which is an additional provision that will mitigate some risk around MRP that results from lease accounting adjustments required for Croxley Business Park.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators FINAL PUBLISHED
findings.headline: External review identified £1.875m in historic MRP overpayments that are being reversed.
findings.detail: Following an external review by MUFG, the council is revising its Minimum Revenue Provision policy and reversing £1.875m of overpayments accumulated over time. MRP charges will also be reduced in the short term. This indicates the council's debt repayment calculations had been systematically incorrect.
findings.matters: A substantial accounting error in MRP—the annual charge that funds debt repayment—was only identified through external review, not internal controls. This is an audit weakness in financial governance.
findings.figures: £1.875m reversal of historic overpayments
findings.quote: The impact of the changes are a reversal of historic MRP overpayments of £1.875m, and reduced MRP Charges in the short term.

findings.paper_title: Minimum Revenue Provision and Prudential Indicators FINAL PUBLISHED
findings.headline: Finance Lease debt operational boundary has been set incorrectly and breached prudential limits.
findings.detail: The council reports a breach of one prudential indicator in 2025/26 affecting Finance Lease debt. The operational boundary was set at a level that does not reflect total external debt including other long-term liabilities as shown in the Capital Strategy. A revised capital strategy will be brought forward for approval.
findings.matters: A breach of a prudential indicator suggests the council's capital control framework is not functioning properly and debt obligations are not being properly tracked. Lenders need confidence that a council's own limits are reliable.
findings.figures: One indicator breach reported; revised capital strategy required
findings.quote: There is a breach of one of the indicators reported in 2025/26 – this relates to the operational boundary for Finance Lease debt, which appears to have been set at a level which does not reflect the total external debt including other long-term liabilities in the Capital Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL
findings.headline: Financing costs are rising as a proportion of net revenue stream, reaching 18.1% by 2026/27.
findings.detail: The proportion of financing costs (interest and minimum revenue provision on borrowing) to net revenue stream increases from 15.58% in 2024/25 actual to 15.90% forecast for 2025/26, then to 18.10% budgeted for 2026/27. This represents a 2.5 percentage point increase over three years, indicating tightening revenue capacity.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and indicate increasing debt service burden. Finance directors use this metric to assess revenue headroom; lenders monitor it as a stress indicator on the council's financial position.
findings.figures: 2024/25 actual 15.58%, 2025/26 forecast 15.90%, 2026/27 budget 18.10%, 2027/28 budget 17.93%; financing costs rising from £2.410m to £3.188m over the period.
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream: 2024/25 actual 15.58%, 2025/26 forecast 15.90%, 2026/27 budget 18.10%, 2027/28 budget 17.93%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators FINAL
findings.headline: Operational boundary for finance leases was incorrectly set 2.5x too low in the Capital Strategy.
findings.detail: The operational boundary for finance lease debt was changed from £275m in 2024/25 to £100m in 2025/26 in error. Actual finance lease debt is £256m, which far exceeds the stated operational boundary. The council acknowledges this error and states a revised Capital Strategy will be brought forward for approval.
findings.matters: This indicates a control weakness in financial planning processes. An operational boundary that does not match actual debt levels defeats its purpose as a management warning tool. Lenders assess governance quality as part of credit analysis.
findings.figures: Actual finance lease debt £256.000m vs operational boundary set at £100m (should have been ~£275m); authorised limit is £300m which provides sufficient headroom.
findings.quote: It appears that an error was made in the preparation of the Capital Strategy for 2025/26; the operational boundary for finance lease debt was changed from £275m in 2024/25 to £100m in 2025/26. As there was no intention to reduce or increase lease debt in the financial plans for 2025/26, this indicator should have been set at a level that allowed for the existing finance lease debt.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy - Appendix 2 - MRP Policy FINAL
findings.headline: Council has made £1.255m cumulative voluntary over-provision specifically to mitigate risks around lease accounting for Croxley Business Park
findings.detail: Watford has deliberately over-provisioned £1.255m in voluntary revenue provision (VRP) beyond its statutory minimum MRP requirement. The council explicitly attributes this entirely to managing risks relating to Croxley Business Park lease accounting. This is a deliberate de-risking decision tied to a specific asset, though the policy document does not disclose what specific risks prompted the over-provision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why a council feels compelled to over-provision debt repayment for a specific lease arrangement. This signals concern about either lease volatility, asset value, or an underlying Croxley Business Park issue that warrants investigation.
findings.figures: £1.255m cumulative VRP overpayment; Finance leases £256.092m of total CFR £339.942m (31.03.2025)
findings.quote: This overpayment has been made specifically to mitigate risks around lease accounting for Croxley Business Park.
